status: agent review, 2026-10-19; a proposal awaiting the researcher's review (D05). Not a researcher decision.
method: Paraphrase check that word-overlap screens cannot do. First pass: four independent model reviewers each read all 1,472 distinct historical questions (topics.HISTORICAL_SOURCES) and one quarter of the 576-question bank, with each bank question's 8 most similar historical and 4 most similar bank questions (TF-IDF over stemmed content words) as hints, and classified every bank question as RESTATEMENT (same phenomenon or question; an answer to one would largely answer the other), CLOSE (same narrow subject, different question), INTERNAL_DUPLICATE, or none; only non-none verdicts are listed. The study author (agent) then rewrote every RESTATEMENT, one question of each INTERNAL_DUPLICATE pair and 23 CLOSE questions judged to share their core answer with a historical question. Second pass: an independent reviewer read both full lists and checked all 88 replacements (one line each). Third pass: the three questions rewritten after the second pass were checked by another independent reviewer; five later rewordings (b1-food-10, b1-health-and-the-body-39, b1-history-33, b1-everyday-science-19, b1-food-24) were checked by the author only.

verdict_meanings.RESTATEMENT: keeps the overlap report unclean while the question is in the bank
verdict_meanings.OK: no historical or bank question asks this

findings.question: How does a mosaic artist choose the size of each tile?
findings.matched: How does a mosaic hold together as an image?
findings.rationale: Both are about how mosaic tesserae read as an image, but one asks about choosing tile size and the other about overall coherence; tile size answers would partly cover coherence.

findings.question: Why do so many cultures use symmetry in decorative patterns?
findings.matched: How does symmetry create a sense of calm while asymmetry creates energy?
findings.rationale: Same narrow subject (symmetry in visual design) but the new question asks why cultures adopt it, not what effect it has, though the calm/order effect is part of either answer.

findings.question: Why do some city squares feel lively while others stay empty?
findings.matched: What separates an inviting public plaza from one that people avoid?
findings.rationale: Both ask what makes some public squares busy and appealing while others stay empty.

findings.question: How does an animator make a drawn figure appear to move smoothly?
findings.matched: How do animators give weight and personality to drawn figures?
findings.rationale: Same practice (animating drawn figures); smooth motion via frames and in-betweens differs from weight and personality, but timing and spacing overlap.

findings.question: Why do architects build small models before building at full size?
findings.matched: How can simulation help engineers test designs before building anything physical?
findings.rationale: Both concern testing a design before full-scale construction, but physical scale models and computer simulation are different practices.

findings.question: Why do many admired paintings use only a narrow range of colours?
findings.matched: Why does a limited palette often produce stronger paintings than unlimited color choices?
findings.rationale: Both ask why paintings using a narrow range of colours succeed.

findings.question: How does a tapestry weaver build a picture thread by thread?
findings.matched: How does a tapestry differ from a painting in the way it is made?
findings.rationale: A good answer on how a tapestry weaver builds a picture thread by thread largely answers how tapestry making differs from painting.

findings.question: Why do art students still draw the human figure from life?
findings.matched: Why is drawing from direct observation still valued when photography exists?
findings.rationale: Drawing the figure from life is drawing from direct observation, and the word 'still' points to the same why-not-photographs question.

findings.question: How does the pattern of brickwork affect the strength of a wall?
findings.matched: Describe why bricklayers stagger the joints in a wall.
findings.rationale: Brickwork bond pattern and wall strength come down to staggered joints spreading load, which is the historical question.

findings.question: Why does the choice of frame affect how a painting is seen?
findings.matched: How does the frame around a picture influence how viewers perceive it?
findings.rationale: Both ask how a frame changes the way a painting is seen.

findings.question: How does a tapestry differ from a painting in the way it is made?
findings.matched: How does a tapestry weaver build a picture thread by thread?
findings.rationale: Explaining how a tapestry differs from a painting in its making mostly means explaining how a weaver builds the picture thread by thread.

findings.question: Why does your reflection appear upside down in the bowl of a spoon?
findings.matched: Why do mirrors reverse left and right but not up and down?
findings.rationale: Same subject (orientation of mirror images) but a concave spoon's inversion is a different optical question from a plane mirror's apparent left-right reversal.

findings.question: How does a liquid thermometer show changes in temperature?
findings.matched: Explain how a spirit thermometer registers a change.
findings.rationale: A spirit thermometer is a liquid thermometer; both ask how liquid expansion shows a temperature change.

findings.question: Why does a kernel of popcorn burst open when heated?
findings.matched: Why does popcorn burst open while other dried grains simply scorch?
findings.rationale: Both ask why popcorn kernels burst when heated (trapped water turning to steam in a sealed hull).

findings.question: Why do your ears pop when driving up a steep hill?
findings.matched: Why do your ears pop when a plane climbs or a car descends a mountain?
findings.rationale: Same phenomenon: ears popping from the air pressure change as altitude changes.

findings.question: How does a magnifying glass make small things look larger?
findings.matched: Explain how a magnifying glass enlarges an image.
findings.rationale: Same question about how a magnifying lens makes things look bigger.

findings.question: Why do clothes on a line dry faster on a windy day?
findings.matched: Why do puddles vanish faster on windy days even when the air stays cool?
findings.rationale: Same causal question: wind carries away humid air at the surface and so speeds evaporation, whether from clothes or puddles.

findings.question: Why do stars twinkle while planets usually shine steadily?
findings.matched: Describe why observatories use adaptive optics.
findings.rationale: Both rest on atmospheric turbulence blurring starlight, but the new question's point (why stars twinkle and planets do not) is different.

findings.question: Why does a metal bridge have small gaps built into its road surface?
findings.matched: Why do bridges and railway tracks include small gaps between their long sections?
findings.rationale: Both ask about expansion gaps in bridges (thermal expansion); 'Describe why bridges are fitted with expansion joints.' [dci/v19/task_bank] matches too.

findings.question: How does a siphon move water up and over the edge of a tank?
findings.matched: Explain how a siphon moves liquid over a rim.
findings.rationale: Same question about how a siphon lifts liquid up and over an edge.

findings.question: Why does an empty room produce echoes that a furnished one does not?
findings.matched: How does a room change the sound of a live performance?
findings.rationale: Both are about room acoustics (reflection and absorption), but the new question asks specifically about empty versus furnished rooms and echo.

findings.question: Why does tyre pressure drop when the weather turns cold?
findings.matched: Why does a balloon shrink when you put it in the freezer?
findings.rationale: Same mechanism (gas in a closed container loses pressure or volume as it cools), so the balloon answer largely covers tyre pressure in cold weather; the objects differ, so this is borderline.

findings.question: Why do sealed snack bags swell up at high altitude?
findings.matched: Why do your ears pop when a plane climbs or a car descends a mountain?
findings.rationale: Both come from lower outside air pressure at altitude acting on a sealed air pocket, but the ear question depends on Eustachian tube physiology.

findings.question: How does a glow stick start to shine when it is bent?
findings.matched: What happens inside a glow stick when you snap it and it lights up?
findings.rationale: Same question about the chemical reaction that makes a bent glow stick shine.

findings.question: Why does stainless steel resist rust when ordinary steel does not?
findings.matched: Describe why steel is galvanised before outdoor use.
findings.rationale: Same narrow subject (protecting steel from rust), but chromium's passive oxide layer works differently from zinc coating.

findings.question: Why does a rolling coin stay upright longer than a still one?
findings.matched: What keeps a spinning top balanced long after a motionless one would fall?
findings.rationale: Same causal question: why a spinning or rolling object stays upright while a still one falls (angular momentum and precession); borderline because rolling also involves bicycle-like steering.

findings.question: Why do aeroplanes leave white trails across a clear sky?
findings.matched: Why can you see your breath on a cold morning but not in summer?
findings.rationale: Contrails are largely the same thing as visible breath (warm moist exhaust condensing in cold air), but they involve aircraft engines and high altitude.

findings.question: Why can water freezing in a pipe split the pipe open?
findings.matched: Describe why potholes form after a cold winter.
findings.rationale: Both rely on water expanding as it freezes, but potholes also involve road wear, so the question is different.

findings.question: Why do washing powders tend to clean better in warm water?
findings.matched: How does soap help water lift grease from a dirty pan?
findings.rationale: Same subject (how detergents clean), but the new question is about why warm water helps.

findings.question: Why does painted wood fade after years in strong sunshine?
findings.matched: Describe why museums dim the lights near old textiles.
findings.rationale: Both turn on light breaking down pigments and causing fading, but one asks why a museum practice exists and the other why painted wood fades.

findings.question: Why do some fabrics crackle with static when pulled off in winter?
findings.matched: Why do some fabrics build up a shock when you pull them apart?
findings.rationale: Same phenomenon: static charge from fabrics rubbing and separating; see also the carpet static question [dci1/v2,dci1v3].

findings.question: Why is lightning seen before the thunder is heard?
findings.matched: Why does thunder arrive noticeably later than the lightning flash that caused it?
findings.rationale: Same question: light travels faster than sound.

findings.question: Why does a whistle produce such a piercing high sound?
findings.matched: Explain how a whistle produces a steady tone.
findings.rationale: Same object; how a whistle makes its tone overlaps with why the tone is high and piercing, but the emphasis differs.

findings.question: How does a pressure cooker cook food faster than an open pan?
findings.matched: How does a pressure cooker shorten cooking time?
findings.rationale: Same question about how a pressure cooker cooks faster (higher boiling point under pressure); 'Explain how a pressure cooker shortens cooking time.' [dci/v19/task_bank] matches too.

findings.question: Why does a car feel hotter inside than the air outside on a sunny day?
findings.matched: Explain how a greenhouse retains warmth for plants.
findings.rationale: A sunny parked car heats up by the greenhouse mechanism (sunlight enters through glass, heat is trapped), so a good greenhouse answer largely answers this; the objects differ.

findings.question: Why does a fridge magnet stay stuck to the door?
findings.matched: Why do magnets grip a steel fridge door yet ignore an aluminum pan?
findings.rationale: Same object (a magnet on a steel fridge door); the historical question's ferromagnetism explanation largely covers why it sticks, so a reviewer might call it a restatement.

findings.question: Why does whipped cream turn into butter if beaten for too long?
findings.matched: Why does whipped cream hold its shape while poured cream does not?
findings.rationale: Same object (whipped cream and fat-globule networks), but over-beating into butter is a different question.

findings.question: How does yeast raise a dough differently from baking powder?
findings.matched: What sets sourdough apart from breads raised with commercial yeast?
findings.rationale: Same narrow subject (how leaveners raise dough), but this compares yeast with chemical baking powder, not sourdough with commercial yeast.

findings.question: Why does sugar turn brown and bitter when heated on its own?
findings.matched: What happens as sugar heats past melting and slides into caramel?
findings.rationale: Both ask what happens chemically when sugar is heated on its own and caramelises.

findings.question: Why do chillies feel hot in the mouth even when they are cold?
findings.matched: Why do chili peppers feel burning hot even though they carry no real heat?
findings.rationale: Same question: capsaicin triggers heat receptors whatever the food's temperature.

findings.question: How does kneading turn a sticky dough smooth and stretchy?
findings.matched: How does kneading develop dough, and why do bakers sometimes stop early?
findings.rationale: Both ask how kneading develops gluten so dough becomes smooth and elastic.

findings.question: How does honey stay edible for such a long time?
findings.matched: Explain how honey resists spoiling for long periods.
findings.rationale: Same question about why honey keeps so long.

findings.question: Why do potatoes turn green when left out in the light?
findings.matched: Describe why potatoes are stored in the dark.
findings.rationale: The reason potatoes are stored in the dark is mainly that light turns them green (chlorophyll and solanine), so the answers largely coincide.

findings.question: How does tempering give chocolate its glossy finish and clean snap?
findings.matched: Why does good chocolate melt so smoothly the moment it hits the tongue?
findings.rationale: Both depend on the cocoa butter crystal form that tempering sets, but gloss and snap differ from melt-in-the-mouth.

findings.question: Why do cooks add starchy cooking water to a sauce?
findings.matched: Why do many cooks save the cloudy water left over from boiling pasta?
findings.rationale: Same practice: starchy pasta water is kept to thicken and emulsify sauces.

findings.question: Why does browned meat taste so different from boiled meat?
findings.matched: How does searing meat change its flavor compared with gently boiling it?
findings.rationale: Same question: browning (Maillard) flavour compared with boiling.

findings.question: Why does a pinch of salt make sweet foods taste sweeter?
findings.matched: How does salt do far more in cooking than simply making dishes salty?
findings.rationale: Salt enhancing sweetness is one part of the broader historical question about salt's roles in cooking.

findings.question: How does milk turn into yoghurt?
findings.matched: What gives fermented foods like yogurt and kimchi their distinctive tang?
findings.rationale: Both turn on lactic acid bacteria in yoghurt, but one asks about the process from milk and the other about the tangy taste.

findings.question: Why are mushrooms so rich in savoury flavour?
findings.matched: Why do cooks treat savory umami as a taste of its own, and which foods supply it richly?
findings.rationale: Same narrow subject (umami-rich foods); mushrooms are a classic example, but the historical question is broader.

findings.question: How does churning while freezing keep ice cream smooth?
findings.matched: How does ice cream stay soft and scoopable instead of freezing solid?
findings.rationale: Same object (ice cream texture); churning, small ice crystals and air overlap with scoopability, but sugar lowering the freezing point is the core of the historical answer.

findings.question: How does a crisp crust form on a loaf as it bakes?
findings.matched: Describe why bread crusts brown in the oven.
findings.rationale: How a crust forms (surface drying and Maillard browning at high temperature) largely answers why crusts brown; borderline because the new question stresses crispness.

findings.question: Why do bakers slash the top of a loaf before it goes in the oven?
findings.matched: Describe why bakeries score the tops of loaves.
findings.rationale: Same practice: slashing or scoring loaves before baking.

findings.question: Why does tea taste bitter if it is left to brew too long?
findings.matched: How do water temperature and steeping time transform the flavor of tea?
findings.rationale: The effect of steeping time on tea (tannins making it bitter) is the core of the historical question.

findings.question: Why do sweet and sour flavours work so well together?
findings.matched: Why do dishes pairing sweet with salty or crisp with soft feel so satisfying?
findings.rationale: Same narrow subject (why contrasting flavour pairings satisfy), but the pairing is sweet with sour, not sweet with salty.

findings.question: How does curing turn a leg of pork into ham?
findings.matched: Why are some hams and cheeses aged for years, and what changes during the wait?
findings.rationale: Same object (ham); curing and long ageing overlap a lot, but the historical question is about the ageing period.

findings.question: Why does street food so often reflect the history of a city?
findings.matched: What makes street food such a beloved centerpiece of eating in many cities?
findings.rationale: Same narrow subject (street food in cities), but the new question asks how it reflects a city's history rather than why it is popular.

findings.question: How does a sourdough starter keep going for years?
findings.matched: Explain how a sourdough starter stays alive between bakes.
findings.rationale: Same question: how a sourdough culture survives and keeps going over time.

findings.question: Why do some cooks salt aubergines before frying them?
findings.matched: How does salt change the texture of vegetables as they cook?
findings.rationale: Both involve salt drawing water out of vegetables by osmosis, but the new question is about the specific practice of salting aubergines before frying.

findings.question: How do hours of gentle cooking make tough meat tender?
findings.matched: What makes tough, well-worked cuts turn silky in a slow braise while lean cuts dry out?
findings.rationale: Same question: long gentle cooking turns collagen in tough cuts into gelatine.

findings.question: How do fjords form along a mountainous coastline?
findings.matched: What makes fjords so distinctive, and how were they carved?
findings.rationale: Both ask how fjords are formed (glacial carving of coastal valleys, later drowned by the sea).

findings.question: How do fjords form along a mountainous coastline?
findings.matched: Why do fjords cut so deeply into some coastlines?
findings.rationale: Both ask how fjords come to be cut into coastlines; one answer (glacial erosion, sea flooding) serves both.

findings.question: Why do monsoon rains arrive at roughly the same time each year?
findings.matched: What makes monsoon rains both a lifeline and a hazard for the regions awaiting them?
findings.rationale: Same subject (monsoon rains) but the new question asks why their timing is regular, not why they help and harm.

findings.question: How do volcanic islands form far from any continent?
findings.matched: How do chains of islands rise from the middle of deep oceans?
findings.rationale: Both ask how volcanic (hotspot / mid-ocean) islands form far out in the ocean.

findings.question: Why does daylight barely change through the year near the equator?
findings.matched: Why do polar regions swing between months of darkness and midnight sun?
findings.rationale: Same mechanism (axial tilt and latitude setting day length), asked from the equator end rather than the poles.

findings.question: How do mapmakers show a round planet on a flat sheet?
findings.matched: How do maps distort the world, and why must flat maps always trade something away?
findings.rationale: Both ask how a round Earth is projected onto a flat map and the compromises that requires.

findings.question: How do sinkholes appear so suddenly in the ground?
findings.matched: What makes limestone country prone to sinkholes, caves, and vanishing rivers?
findings.rationale: The historical question covers sinkhole formation in soluble rock; the new one focuses on why collapse is sudden, so substantial overlap.

findings.question: How does permafrost affect building in the coldest regions?
findings.matched: How do communities adapt to living above the tree line or on permafrost?
findings.rationale: Same subject (living and building on permafrost), but the historical question is broader community adaptation.

findings.question: Why do seaside towns rarely see extreme temperatures?
findings.matched: Why do temperatures swing more widely in places far from the ocean?
findings.rationale: Same maritime-versus-continental moderation effect, seen from the coast side; also matches "How does distance from the sea shape how extreme a region's seasons become?" [dci1/v2,dci1v3].

findings.question: Why do thick fogs regularly roll in along certain coasts?
findings.matched: Why do some coastal towns experience fog far more often than places inland?
findings.rationale: Both ask why certain coasts get frequent fog (cold currents/sea surface cooling moist air).

findings.question: Why do some places have daylight at midnight in summer?
findings.matched: Why do polar regions swing between months of darkness and midnight sun?
findings.rationale: Both ask why high-latitude places get the midnight sun in summer (axial tilt).

findings.question: How do coral atolls come to form rings around a lagoon?
findings.matched: Why are coral reefs confined to particular waters, and how do they build up?
findings.rationale: Same object (coral reefs); atoll ring formation around a sinking island is a more specific question than how reefs build up.

findings.question: Why are mountain tops colder even though they are nearer the sun?
findings.matched: How does climbing in altitude change the climate even close to the equator?
findings.rationale: Both turn on why air gets colder with altitude (lapse rate, thinner air), regardless of nearness to the sun.

findings.question: Why do fjords cut so deeply into some coastlines?
findings.matched: What makes fjords so distinctive, and how were they carved?
findings.rationale: Asking why fjords cut so deep is answered by how they were glacially carved.

findings.question: Why do fjords cut so deeply into some coastlines?
findings.matched: How do fjords form along a mountainous coastline?
findings.rationale: Both ask how fjords come to be cut into coastlines; one answer serves both.

findings.question: Why do some mountain valleys have strong winds at the same hour each day?
findings.matched: Why are certain valleys prone to trapping cold air?
findings.rationale: Same object (mountain valley air flows driven by daily heating and cooling), but daily valley winds differ from cold-air pooling.

findings.question: Why are some islands still rising out of the sea?
findings.matched: How do chains of islands rise from the middle of deep oceans?
findings.rationale: Islands rising out of the sea could be read as volcanic island growth (overlapping) or uplift/rebound (different).

findings.question: What causes pins and needles in an arm or leg?
findings.matched: Why does a foot go numb after sitting cross-legged for too long?
findings.rationale: Pins and needles and a foot going numb after sitting cross-legged are the same nerve-compression phenomenon.

findings.question: Why does yawning seem to spread from one person to another?
findings.matched: Why do people yawn when they see someone else yawning?
findings.rationale: Both ask why yawning is contagious.

findings.question: Why does a foot go numb after sitting cross-legged for too long?
findings.matched: What causes pins and needles in an arm or leg?
findings.rationale: A numb foot from sitting cross-legged is the pins-and-needles nerve-compression phenomenon.

findings.question: Why does laughing make people feel good?
findings.matched: How does laughter affect the body beyond simply lifting the mood?
findings.rationale: Same subject (effects of laughter), but the historical question explicitly asks about effects beyond mood, which the new one asks about.

findings.question: How does the immune system remember an infection it has met before?
findings.matched: Describe how vaccines train immune memory in general terms.
findings.rationale: Both are answered by the same account of memory B and T cells enabling a faster second response.

findings.question: How do muscles grow stronger after repeated hard use?
findings.matched: How does the body adapt over weeks when someone starts strength training?
findings.rationale: Both ask how muscles adapt and strengthen under repeated hard use.

findings.question: Why does sleep help people remember what they learned during the day?
findings.matched: Why does a good night's sleep improve mood, focus, and patience the next day?
findings.rationale: Same subject (benefits of sleep), but memory consolidation is a different question from mood and focus.

findings.question: Why does the body raise its temperature during an infection?
findings.matched: How does fever help the body fight infection even though it feels awful?
findings.rationale: Both ask why the body raises its temperature during infection.

findings.question: Why does the heart rate stay raised for a while after exercise?
findings.matched: What happens to the heart and lungs during a sustained bout of aerobic exercise?
findings.rationale: Same subject (heart response to exercise), but the new question is about recovery after exercise, not during it.

findings.question: How does blood clot to stop a small cut from bleeding?
findings.matched: Why does a scab form over a cut as it heals?
findings.rationale: A scab is a dried clot, so the answers overlap heavily, though the new question is about stopping bleeding rather than healing.

findings.question: Why does a bump on the head swell up so quickly?
findings.matched: Why does a twisted ankle swell up?
findings.rationale: Both ask why a minor impact injury swells (inflammation and fluid leaking from damaged vessels).

findings.question: Why do some people get seasick while others are untroubled?
findings.matched: Why does motion sickness strike some travellers and spare others?
findings.rationale: Seasickness is motion sickness; both ask why some people suffer and others do not.

findings.question: Why does your own voice sound strange when played back?
findings.matched: Why does your recorded voice sound so unlike the voice you hear while speaking?
findings.rationale: Both ask why your recorded voice sounds strange to you (bone conduction).

findings.question: Why does a twisted ankle swell up?
findings.matched: Why does a bump on the head swell up so quickly?
findings.rationale: Both ask why a minor injury swells (inflammatory fluid build-up).

findings.question: How did taming the horse change how far people could travel?
findings.matched: In what ways did taming horses transform how societies fought, traded, and traveled?
findings.rationale: The historical question covers horse domestication and travel; the new question is a narrower part of it.

findings.question: How did the plough change early farming communities?
findings.matched: What made improved plows and harnesses so significant for medieval farming?
findings.rationale: Same object (the plough and farming), but early versus medieval farming communities.

findings.question: Why did lighthouses become so important to seaborne trade?
findings.matched: Explain how a lighthouse helps ships navigate at night.
findings.rationale: Same object; the historical question is about how a lighthouse works, the new one about its role in trade.

findings.question: How did the spread of reading among ordinary people change society?
findings.matched: How did the spread of printing change who could join public debate?
findings.rationale: Close subject (spread of literacy and print), but the new question is about reading among ordinary people and its effect on society.

findings.question: Why did early railways push towns to agree on a shared clock time?
findings.matched: How did the standardisation of time affect travel?
findings.rationale: Same episode (railway-driven time standardisation) seen as cause rather than effect; answers would overlap a lot.

findings.question: How did windmills and watermills change daily labour?
findings.matched: Explain how a windmill turns grain into flour.
findings.rationale: Same object (mills), but how they work differs from their effect on labour.

findings.question: Why did castles gradually fall out of use?
findings.matched: Why did stone castles gradually lose their military value as gunpowder weapons improved?
findings.rationale: Both ask why castles fell out of use; the gunpowder answer dominates both.

findings.question: How did free public libraries change access to learning?
findings.matched: Describe how public libraries support local communities.
findings.rationale: Same object (public libraries), historical versus present-day framing of access and support.

findings.question: How did the potato change population growth in the lands it reached?
findings.matched: How did the exchange of crops and animals between hemispheres reshape diets and economies?
findings.rationale: The potato is a central case of the crop exchange, but the new question is about population growth specifically.

findings.question: Why did early sailors seek new sea routes to the spice markets?
findings.matched: Why were spices once so precious that nations fought wars over their trade?
findings.rationale: Same subject (the spice trade); the value of spices partly answers why sailors sought sea routes, but the route-seeking question is distinct.

findings.question: How did banking grow out of the habits of early merchants?
findings.matched: Why did expanding trade push merchants to invent banking, credit, and insurance?
findings.rationale: Both ask how banking grew out of merchant trading practices.

findings.question: How did public sewers change life in growing cities?
findings.matched: How did clean water and sewer projects transform life in crowded industrial cities?
findings.rationale: Both ask how public sewer systems changed life in growing cities.

findings.question: How did the arrival of radio change family evenings at home?
findings.matched: In what ways did radio broadcasting change politics between the world wars?
findings.rationale: Same object (radio's social impact), but domestic leisure versus politics.

findings.question: How did the first universities come into being?
findings.matched: How did the first universities emerge in medieval towns, and whom did they serve?
findings.rationale: Both ask how the first universities came into being.

findings.question: How did the magnetic compass change long sea voyages?
findings.matched: How did advances in navigation let sailors venture far beyond familiar coastlines?
findings.rationale: The compass is a key navigation advance, so answers overlap, but the historical question is broader.

findings.question: How does a mystery novel keep readers guessing until the end?
findings.matched: How do writers create suspense while still playing fair with the reader?
findings.rationale: 'Playing fair with the reader' is mystery-genre language, so answers overlap heavily (clues, misdirection), though the historical item is about suspense in general.

findings.question: Why can tone of voice change the meaning of a remark?
findings.matched: How can the same sentence carry very different meanings depending on tone of voice?
findings.rationale: Both ask how tone of voice changes the meaning of the same words.

findings.question: How does sarcasm work when the listener has only the voice to go on?
findings.matched: What happens to meaning when sarcasm moves from speech to text?
findings.rationale: Same narrow subject (vocal cues to sarcasm); one asks how it works in speech, the other what is lost in text, so answers partly overlap.

findings.question: Why do some stories begin in the middle of the action?
findings.matched: What makes some openings of novels pull readers in immediately?
findings.rationale: Both are about story openings; starting in the middle of the action is one way an opening hooks readers, but the new question is narrower.

findings.question: Why do dictionaries keep adding new entries every year?
findings.matched: How does a dictionary decide what to include?
findings.rationale: Same object (dictionary inclusion); answers both rest on evidence of usage, though one asks why entries keep growing and the other about inclusion criteria.

findings.question: How does an author decide how a story should end?
